title: C: Diamond-like-carbon nanoimprint masters replace EUV on array layers
idea: Coat quartz nanoimprint templates with a ta-C/DLC wear layer to extend template life ~10x, then imprint the strictly periodic DRAM array layers (active, buried wordline, storage node) while DUV handles periphery.
why: Removes 3-5 EUV exposures per wafer at ~1/10 tool cost and power, and breaks the single-supplier EUV dependence.

title: Eliminate leading-edge wafers for legacy demand: restart mothballed DUV lines
idea: Eliminate serving DDR3/DDR4/LPDDR4 demand from leading-edge fabs: acquire mothballed or exiting 300mm lines and run 2x-nm DUV-only DRAM (zero EUV) for auto, industrial and networking, so leading fabs stop diverting wafers to legacy parts.
why: Legacy parts are rising fastest in price; a depreciated DUV line costs ~10-20% of greenfield per wafer start and avoids the single-supplier EUV chokepoint.

title: Non-power-of-two partial-good DRAM dies with OS bad-bank maps
idea: Worse: scrap every die with a failed bank or sub-array beyond the repair fuses. Flip: sell 12/20/28 Gb harvested dies with whole banks fused off, publishing a bad-bank map in SPD that memory controllers and the OS honor, the way CPU vendors harvest cores.
why: Recovers dies that are scrap today: usable bits per wafer up ~3-8% at zero capex.

title: Magnify supplier count 10x with open-source DRAM IP
idea: Fund a DARPA-style open, royalty-free gain-cell memory macro, controller RTL and process module portable to any 22-40 nm logic fab, with qualified PDK decks for GlobalFoundries, TI, SkyWater-class and Intel 16, so ~30 mature logic fabs can make DRAM-class memory chiplets.
why: Breaks the 3-supplier oligopoly and the 1-2% U.S. share; taps idle mature-node capacity for capacity-tier memory without new fabs.

title: Ice pack: printed thermoelectric film chills salvaged DIMMs for retention
idea: Random stimulus 'ice pack' -> cool it to keep it fresh. An R2R printed Bi2Te3/Sb2Te3 thermoelectric film is laminated between DIMM and heat spreader to hold die 10-15 C below their uncooled temperature, doubling to tripling retention time.
why: Lets weak salvaged or fallout die pass retention and cuts refresh energy (fact 3) ~50%; raises reuse yield cheaply.

title: Magnify sharing: rack-wide content-addressed memory deduplication
idea: A CXL memory fabric hashes every 4 KB page and keeps one physical copy rack-wide of identical model weights, container images, libraries and zero pages with copy-on-write, so inference fleets running one model on 64-128 accelerators share a single copy.
why: For weight-dominated AI fleets, usable GB per physical GB rises ~50-100x, cutting effective cost per usable GB ~100x.

title: Time-shared EUV: consortium scanners rented by the hour
idea: Rearrange ownership of the scarcest tool: a consortium fab hosts EUV scanners and tracks. DRAM startups send sealed lots in for the 5-7 EUV critical layers only and do every other step in their own lower-cost fabs.
why: EUV has one supplier and costs $200M+ per tool. Entrants avoid buying scanners, cutting entry capex by ~$1-2B and raising scanner utilization.

title: Mid-process wafer bank: park front-end wafers, finish during spikes
idea: Time shift inside the fab: during gluts, process wafers through the capacitor module and store them in nitrogen stockers. When a shortage hits, run only the back-end layers, cutting fab-out time from ~3 months to ~3 weeks.
why: Turns slack fab time in a glut into ready supply for a shortage. The cycle-time cut lets output follow demand spikes; needs only N2 purge.

title: Eliminate the 85C margin: cold-only DRAM grade for liquid racks
idea: Eliminate the worst-case temperature spec: dies failing at 85-95C but passing at 45C are certified Cold-Grade for direct-liquid-cooled racks with guaranteed coolant temperature and on-DIMM thermal shutdown; $1M funds binning, sensors and one data-center pilot.
why: Retention roughly doubles per ~10C cooler, so thermal-screen rejects become usable bits as liquid cooling spreads.

title: No silicon wafer: monolithic oxide tiers multiply panel density
idea: Forced limit: panels cannot shrink to DRAM litho. Stack 8-32 monolithic IGZO gain-cell tiers on glass at 350 C or below, each tier self-aligned to the one below with shared staircase contacts.
why: Density: tiers instead of nodes multiply bits per panel by up to 32x, reaching the roughly 26-tier break-even on cheap glass.

title: H: Croconic-acid hydrogen-bond ferroelectric memory from carbon, hydrogen, oxygen
idea: Croconic acid (C5H2O5) switches polarization by proton transfer along hydrogen bonds (Pr ~20-30 uC/cm2 at room temperature); evaporate it below 150 C onto any CMOS BEOL as non-volatile capacitors.
why: Fully abundant C, H, O and a low-temperature process enable distributed manufacturing.

title: Downhole-and-orbit beachhead funds a domestic DRAM learning curve
idea: Extreme users at 200 C downhole and in rad-hard space and defense pay 50-200x commodity $/bit, so a small U.S. 90-65 nm SOI trench-DRAM line can be profitable at a few thousand wafers a year. Margins fund a planned descent through nodes toward commercial sockets, the way GaN moved from radar to phone chargers.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability (1-2% share): premium niches pay for the learning curve instead of a $15B+ upfront bet.

title: Cr: Chromia magnetoelectric memory written by voltage, not current
idea: Boron-doped Cr2O3 films (Neel temperature raised above 400 K) flip their boundary magnetization with an electric field plus small bias field, read by anomalous Hall in an adjacent Fe layer.
why: Voltage writes cost ~100x less energy than STT; chromium is abundant and recyclable from stainless steel.

title: Nuclear-plant co-located DRAM fab with utility rate-base financing
idea: Fuse an existing nuclear plant (or new SMR cluster) with a DRAM fab on the same site. Firm 24/7 carbon-free power comes in at cost, and condenser waste heat preheats ultrapure water and HVAC makeup air. The utility finances the power and water infrastructure as a regulated asset.
why: Fab power is about 5-10% of wafer cost and the shell and utilities about 20% of capex. This cuts both by an estimated 20-40% and de-risks U.S. siting.

title: Pre-built cleanroom shell bank leased to any memory entrant
idea: Time shift of construction: the government builds standardized 300 mm cleanroom shells with power, ultrapure water and gas yards years before anyone needs them, then leases them turnkey to the first memory maker that commits tools.
why: Cuts time to first wafer from ~4 years to ~18 months and removes ~30% of fab capex from the entrant's balance sheet. Directly raises U.S. manufacturability.

title: Counter-cyclical tool bank: buy lithography and etch tools in downturns
idea: Time shift of tool procurement: a cooperative buys DRAM process tools while vendors discount them in a downturn, keeps them crated in bonded climate-controlled warehouses, and leases them out when the upturn comes.
why: Tool lead times of 12-24 months are a hidden ramp bottleneck. A tool bank cuts ramp time by ~1 year and tool cost by 15-30%.

title: DRAM veterans corps: retired Qimonda/Elpida engineers seed U.S. fabs
idea: Time shift of know-how: recruit retired DRAM process and yield engineers into a paid mentor corps embedded in new U.S. fabs, and record their tacit knowledge as recipe playbooks and video so it survives them.
why: The U.S. lacks DRAM process talent. Compressing the yield learning curve from ~3 years to ~18 months is worth billions in early-life scrap.

title: Continuous Czochralski: one crucible pulls 8 ingots instead of one
idea: Time shift of crucible life: adapt solar-industry continuous CZ (granular polysilicon fed in while pulling) to 300 mm prime wafers, so one crucible survives several ingot pulls over ~2 weeks.
why: Crucible consumption, and the Spruce Pine quartz it embodies, falls ~5-8x per wafer, and puller utilization rises ~20%.

title: Vendor-owned memory leasing with socketed, design-for-disassembly packages
idea: Ownership time shift: vendors lease DRAM by GB-year rather than selling it, and ship socketed, solder-free packages so they can recall, retest and re-lease the same die over 10-15 years across 3 server generations.
why: Vendors earn on lifetime use rather than one sale, so durability becomes an incentive. The installed die base works 2-3x longer, which multiplies effective supply.

title: Cross-generation CXL reuse of retired DDR4 as tier-2 memory
idea: Time shift of DIMM life: a CXL controller with a DDR4 back end and strong symbol ECC lets hyperscalers move DDR4 pulled from retired servers into CXL boxes attached to new DDR5-only CPUs.
why: Delays e-waste of DIMMs with plenty of life left by 4-6 years. Covers 20-30% of new-server capacity needs without new bits.

title: LTS-DRAM: freeze one interface for 15 years so old fabs never retire
idea: Decade time shift of standards: JEDEC freezes a long-term-support DRAM interface (DDR4-compatible) guaranteed for 15 years, so fully depreciated legacy fabs keep running and platforms keep accepting their parts.
why: Once depreciation (~55% of wafer cost) reaches zero, legacy bits get very cheap. Keeping that capacity alive instead of scrapping it preserves ~10-15% of world wafer starts.

title: Move burn-in and retention screening into the first weeks of deployment
idea: Time shift of testing: ship DRAM after a short wafer sort. On-module BIST and the host memory controller run retention, row-hammer and burn-in sweeps during each server's first 2 weeks in service, and parts that fail are mapped out or swapped.
why: Test equipment and burn-in ovens are a capacity chokepoint. This frees ~30-50% of test capacity and cuts test cost per bit ~5%.

title: V-formation consortium rotating the costly node-development lead
idea: Geese take turns flying at the front of the V, where drag is worst. In a U.S./allied DRAM consortium, members take turns funding and running pathfinding for each new node or cell concept, and every member licenses the result at cost.
why: Splits ~$2-4B per-node R&D across members so smaller players keep pace, raising the number of suppliers.

title: Pick-n-pull robotic DRAM package harvesting from consumer e-waste
idea: Copying the auto-junkyard 'pick-n-pull' model at component scale, a robotic line X-rays scrapped phones and laptops, selectively reflows only the LPDDR/DDR packages with a hot-gas nozzle, reballs them, and mounts them on standard CXL carrier cards with a small controller that hides package heterogeneity.
why: Turns e-waste (billions of devices, ~8 GB each) into a U.S. domestic memory source; scarce-resource and capital intensity near zero, cost per usable bit maybe 25-40% of new.

title: Retired GPUs repurposed as HBM memory appliances for newer accelerators
idea: Inverts 'an accelerator is worthless once its compute is obsolete': older GPUs stay in racks as 80-141 GB HBM memory servers, reached by newer accelerators over NVLink/CXL fabrics for KV-cache and parameter offload, their compute used only for copy and compression.
why: HBM scarcity: reuses HBM stacks that cannot be desoldered, adding terabytes of high-bandwidth far memory per rack without new HBM wafers.

title: Maskless DMD diode-laser exposure for all non-critical DRAM layers
idea: Scale shift of the mask: micromirror arrays steer 375-405 nm diode lasers to expose implant, pad, redistribution and bump layers digitally, retiring the KrF excimer scanners and photomasks those layers use.
why: Removes krypton and neon from ~30-40% of exposure layers and cuts mask spend ~20%. Design changes take a file swap instead of a mask.

title: Space-style anneal bake to rejuvenate aged DRAM
idea: Spacecraft engineers know total-dose and hot-carrier damage partly anneals at elevated temperature. A 10-person refurb shop bakes retired DRAM packages at 150-200 C for 24-168 h, below reflow, to recover interface-trap-driven retention and timing loss, then retests and upgrades the bin.
why: Could raise the share of harvested modules passing full spec from ~70% to 85-90%.

title: No server may own its RAM: spot market per GB-second
idea: Self-imposed limit: memory is only rented. A CXL-switched rack pool runs an internal exchange where VMs bid for capacity by the GB-second. Stranded memory, which is 25-50% of provisioned DRAM in clouds, is auctioned back within milliseconds via page migration.
why: Do the job with less: cuts the DRAM provisioned per server by 10-25% fleet-wide through price signals rather than static sizing.

title: Dynamics: flex-fab with rail-mounted tool pods reconfiguring routes in weeks
idea: TRIZ #15 Dynamics: tools sit in standardized mobile pods on floor rails with quick-connect utilities, and the AMHS route is software-defined, so a line can re-balance between HBM, DDR5 and LPDDR process variants in weeks as prices move.
why: Supply responsiveness: shrinks the mismatch between price signals and output from quarters to weeks.

title: Retention-reject DRAM regraded with a weak-row fast-refresh buffer
idea: Ideal: every die that works at all gets sold. Closest achievable with no new fab: dies failing 64 ms retention because of the leakage tail are binned as a 16 ms grade, and a 40 nm module buffer refreshes only the profiled weak rows, using a map stored in on-module flash at test.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): recovers 2-5% of wafer output for a small refresh-energy cost.

title: Plated-Wire NDRO Memory Made on Magnet-Wire Lines, Read Without Restore
idea: Revive the plated-wire memory of the UNIVAC 1110 and Viking-era spacecraft (permalloy electroplated on beryllium-copper wire, read non-destructively): continuous wire-plating lines like U.S. magnet-wire plants plate CoFe/NiFe on 25 um wires woven with drive straps, and each read senses only the addressed word's magnetization tilt with a tiny pulse and no restore.
why: Destructive read and overfetch (fact 8): word-sized non-destructive reads at ~0.2-0.5 pJ/bit, >=10x below DRAM activate-plus-restore; new supply from the wire industry.

title: Circular DRAM leasing with manufacturer take-back and re-binning
idea: Fuse equipment-leasing finance with memory. Makers lease DIMMs and HBM cards by GB-month and keep ownership. At end of lease they recover the modules, re-bin them by measured retention and speed, and redeploy them down a tiered ladder: hyperscale, then enterprise, then edge.
why: Doubles or triples each bit's productive life and gives makers annuity revenue that smooths cycles. Effective supply rises with no wafer starts.

title: ZettaCore's molecules applied last: multi-bit redox cells on 180 nm
idea: ZettaCore's porphyrin molecular memory (several discrete charge states per molecule in a DRAM-like cell) died before it was integrated into a production flow, partly because molecules had to survive hot back-end steps. Fix: attach the redox-molecule monolayer as the final low-temperature step on finished 180 nm CMOS wafers and read 3-4 discrete oxidation states per cell, giving ~2 bits per cell.
why: Density and charge wall: redox states store charge at fixed potentials, giving more charge per area than a planar capacitor and ~2x bits per cell at an old node.

title: Phone-refurbisher robotic harvesting of soldered LPDDR and GDDR
idea: Adapted from smartphone refurbishing lines: scrapped laptops, GPUs, consoles and phones are X-ray mapped, memory packages are freed by laser-assisted selective reflow and picked, robots reball them, and high-parallel testers burn them in before they are rebuilt into LPCAMM/SODIMM modules.
why: Hundreds of millions of devices with soldered DRAM retire each year; recovering ~10% of them could add a few % of annual bit supply with almost no fab capital (scarce resources, supply).

title: Partial action: Lego-fab adding 2,500-wafer modules as demand appears
idea: TRIZ #16 Partial action: rather than one $15B mega-fab, build containerized prefab cleanroom modules each sized for ~2,500 wspm of a fixed mature DRAM flow, adding modules in 9-month increments.
why: Capital intensity and cycle risk: lowers entry ticket to ~$1-2B and avoids overbuild at cycle peaks.

title: Retention-tier binning: weak-retention dies for short-lived data
idea: Reverse the retention spec: dies that miss 64 ms retention are binned by measured retention (16/32 ms), not discarded. They go to workloads whose data is rewritten before it decays (AI activations, KV-cache pages rewritten every few ms), and the controller sets refresh per module and skips it for fresh data.
why: Gets back dies lost to the leakage tail (fact 3), adding several percent of good-die output. Refresh energy for short-lived data drops toward zero.

title: HBM stack reclaim from accelerators with dead logic dies
idea: Extreme user: 100k-GPU clusters where the GPU dies but its HBM stacks are healthy. A 10-person lab uses localized laser debond and thermocompression to lift stacks off failed interposers, re-bump them and mount 2-4 per card on low-cost organic substrates with an FPGA HBM controller.
why: HBM takes ~3x the wafer area per bit of DDR5 (fact 6); salvaging stacks recovers the scarcest bits.

title: Universal die: one DRAM die, fuse-selectable DDR5, LPDDR5 or GDDR
idea: Ideal: any wafer becomes whatever bit type is short. Closest achievable on existing lines: a die with a multi-protocol PHY and fuse/firmware-selectable bank organization is configured at packaging, so fabs stop guessing product mix 6 months ahead.
why: Mix-mismatch shortages: ~5-10% more effective supply through fungibility for ~3-5% die-area cost.

title: Gen-8.5 display fabs printing stacked IGZO gain-cell memory sheets
idea: Ideal: memory printed by the square meter like wallpaper. Closest achievable with no new fab: idle LCD/OLED TFT fabs (2.2x2.5 m glass, IGZO already in production) build 3-4 stacked layers of 2T0C IGZO gain cells at 2 bits per cell, diced into slow-tier memory tiles (~100 ns-1 us) behind a controller.
why: Uses the world's largest idle lithography area with no EUV: ~10 GB per panel per layer at 1.5 um rules, maybe $3-8/GB with stacking; density and speed are the risk.

title: Minify reliability to 1e-3 BER: junk-tolerant stacked memory
idea: Sell memory for noise-tolerant AI tensors at a raw 1e-3 bit error rate: skip sort, burn-in, repair and final test, let each die self-map defects via boot-time BIST, and absorb errors with stochastic rounding and error-resilient training.
why: Dropping the yield gate lets fabs stack 64 cheap thin-film cell layers whose compound yield would otherwise be near zero, and removes ~25-40% test/repair cost; together these target ~100x lower $/GB.

title: Recompute-grade DRAM SKU priced by verified raw bit-error rate
idea: Extreme user: AI KV-cache and activations are recomputable, so a bit flip costs a recompute, not a crash. Fabs ship dies that fail strict screens at a guaranteed raw BER (e.g., 1e-10 per bit-hour); inference stacks add per-block checksums and recompute on mismatch, and buyers pay per verified-good GB-hour.
why: Turns statistical-screen fallout into supply and lets buyers drop ECC overhead; perhaps 3-8% more sellable bits per wafer.

title: Advance market commitment for non-DRAM byte-addressable tiers
idea: Box[Owner=hyperscaler consortium x Finance=advance market commitment x Medium=any byte-addressable memory meeting latency and endurance specs x Channel=guaranteed purchase volume]: buyers commit a fixed purchase volume at a set price to any supplier that hits ~100 ns access and 10^15 endurance, like vaccine AMCs.
why: Pulls new memory technologies to volume; de-risks entrant fabs and diversifies supply away from DRAM.

title: Wafer as a stamp: layer-transfer arrays, reuse the donor wafer
idea: Reverse the wafer from consumable to reusable template: grow a crystalline device layer on a porous-Si or ion-cut donor and transfer it to a cheap carrier. The donor is re-polished and reused 10+ times.
why: Cuts the water for crystal pulling, slicing and polishing ~10x per wafer. Reusing donors also cuts demand for Spruce Pine quartz crucibles.

title: Federated yield-learning commons on anonymized wafer maps
idea: Worse: let every fab relearn the same defect signatures in secret. Flip: fabs train shared defect-classification models by federated learning on local wafer maps and inspection images so only weights leave each site, and new entrants receive the pre-trained model free.
why: Pulls new-line yield ramps in by months; yield-limited supply rises.

title: Copy-exact fab franchising licensed by an incumbent
idea: Ideal: a new fab appears as easily as installing software. Closest achievable: an incumbent franchises a frozen, copy-exact DRAM process plus fab design to sovereign or partner builders for royalties and equity, McDonald's style, with incumbent teams running the ramp.
why: Time to capacity and talent: ramp falls from 3-5 years to ~2, and the number of builders multiplies.

title: Hodgkin-Huxley NDR bistable cell: transistor plus tunnel-diode pair
idea: Sodium channels give the membrane an N-shaped I-V curve, which makes it bistable. A Goto pair of tunnel or resonant-tunneling diodes latches a node into one of two stable states behind one access transistor, using an Esaki-junction module added to a logic process.
why: SRAM-like unlimited endurance and no refresh with 2-3 devices per cell instead of 6, and no capacitor; standby current is the risk.

title: Minify masks to zero: million-beam maskless write for micro-fabs
idea: Use multi-beam e-beam writers (~1M beams) to direct-write the 3-5 critical layers in regional low-volume DRAM fabs, eliminating $10-20M mask sets and making custom memory runs economical.
why: Cuts capital and mask cost for small fabs; makes low-volume, domain-specific memory variants viable.

title: Supercritical-CO2-swellable mold compound frees bare dies for repackaging
idea: Encapsulant is a thermoplastic designed for high CO2 solubility that swells and loses adhesion in scCO2 at 31 C and 74 bar. Retired packages are soaked and rapidly depressurized, delaminating to release intact dies without acids.
why: Bare-die recovery enables re-binning into new packages and stacks, unlike acid decapsulation that destroys dies.

title: Regulated-utility rate base for a domestic memory utility
idea: Adapted from electric utility regulation: a public commission grants a U.S. DRAM fab a regulated ~8-9% return on its rate base, with guaranteed offtake by federal and critical-infrastructure buyers at cost-of-service prices.
why: Lowers the cost of capital and removes cyclicality for one or two U.S. baseline fabs, cutting cost per bit ~10-20% against merchant financing while guaranteeing domestic supply (capital, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Pay depreciated DRAM lines to keep running instead of converting
idea: A fully depreciated line's wafer cost is ~45% of a new one because depreciation is ~55% of cost. Governments or buyer consortia pay fabs to keep old 1x/1y-nm lines producing for 5 more years rather than converting them to HBM or scrapping tools, with guaranteed offtake covering the opportunity cost.
why: Cost per bit and supply: preserves the cheapest bits on Earth, adding ~10% supply at ~50% of new-node cost.

title: No silicon wafer: federal guaranteed offtake for first non-Si memory
idea: Forced limit: the first buyers must be guaranteed. Federal agencies pre-commit to buy a fixed volume of qualified non-Si memory modules at a set price for five years, as Operation Warp Speed did for vaccines.
why: Removes demand risk that stops investors funding unproven substrates; brings first capacity forward by years.

title: Eliminate repeat qualification: shared reliability dataset for substitute DRAM
idea: Eliminate 12-24-month per-OEM requalification when switching DRAM sources: a consortium runs one automotive-grade stress dataset per part (HTOL, temperature cycling, ESD) and shares it under a common audit, so members switch to available parts in weeks; $1M funds lab time for ~40 parts.
why: Makes existing alternative supply usable quickly instead of waiting for a qualified part.

title: UCIe memory chiplet marketplace for small-fab memories
idea: Box[Integration=UCIe die-to-die memory chiplet profile x Medium=any (eDRAM, oxide, MRAM) x Owner=open standards body x Channel=certified chiplet catalog]: define a memory-chiplet protocol so small fabs can sell interchangeable working-memory chiplets to any SoC maker.
why: Supply diversification: opens a channel for many smaller fabs and new media to add bits outside the big three.

title: Cloud RAM surge pricing shifts demand to memory-light SKUs
idea: Box[Channel=cloud instance pricing x Finance=dynamic $/GB-hour indexed to DRAM contract price x Integration=standard servers]: clouds price RAM separately from vCPU and raise it in shortages, steering tenants to memory-light configs, while freed DIMMs are re-provisioned in standard slots.
why: Demand response: an estimated 10-20% cut in peak DRAM demand during shortages with no hardware change.

title: Federal tool-loan bank inserts DRAM tool sets into idle U.S. logic fabs
idea: Inverts 'DRAM needs a purpose-built DRAM fab': a federal bank buys and loans DRAM-specific tool sets (capacitor etch, high-k ALD, cell implant) to underused U.S. 300 mm logic fabs that run a licensed 1x-nm DRAM flow.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: reuses existing cleanroom shells and utilities at roughly 1/3 the capex and 2-3 years faster than greenfield.

title: Piggy bank: Treasury memory bonds indexed to DRAM contract prices
idea: Random stimulus 'piggy bank' -> households save to hedge. Retail 'Memory I-Bonds' pay a coupon that tracks a DRAM contract-price index; proceeds become low-cost loans for US DRAM fabs, and households hedge the device-cost inflation shortages cause.
why: Cheap patient capital for capital-intensive fabs ($15B+) and a public hedge that politically sustains US capacity.

title: Catch-muscle antiferroelectric gate transistor in any HKMG fab
idea: Mollusc catch muscle locks tension while using almost no energy. A Zr-rich HfZrO antiferroelectric gate layer, biased by a work-function offset into a stable latch inside its double hysteresis loop, gives a 1T cell whose threshold voltage holds the state; every high-k/metal-gate fab already has HfO2 ALD.
why: Antiferroelectric switching endurance may reach 1e12-1e14 cycles versus ~1e10 for ferroelectrics; 1T and capacitorless on existing tools.

title: All-dry back end: stealth laser dicing and plasma thinning
idea: Replace water-cooled blade dicing and wet grind/polish with stealth laser dicing (internal modification, then tape expansion) and dry plasma thinning. Dry plasma activation replaces wet cleans before hybrid bonding.
why: Cuts back-end DI water (dicing, grinding, post-grind cleans) >10x. Laser dicing also narrows the streets between dies, adding ~2-5% more dies per wafer.

title: Via-last HBM TSVs etched in existing MEMS fabs
idea: Ideal: the DRAM fab spends nothing on TSVs. Closest achievable with no new fab: TSV etch, liner, fill and thinning move from DRAM fabs to existing 200/300mm MEMS and power fabs that already run Bosch DRIE, using a via-last flow with landing pads designed into the periphery.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): frees DRAM-fab tool time and can shrink keep-out area, using idle trailing capacity.

title: Test in the field: ship lightly tested dies, repair at boot
idea: Rearrange where testing happens: cut wafer and package test time ~70%. In-system BIST, post-package-repair fuses and runtime ECC telemetry then find and repair weak cells at first boot and over the product's life.
why: Testers are a capacity bottleneck and a large cost. Moving test into the field frees tester capacity and raises output ~5-10%.

title: Tera MTA's latency tolerance puts slow 180 nm memory to work
idea: Tera Computer's MTA (1990s) hid memory latency with 128 hardware threads per processor and no data caches, but lost the market. Fix: pair latency-tolerant multithreaded accelerators with memory built on 180 nm lines (~150-300 ns access), so slow but buildable bits do throughput work (graph analytics, sparse math, retrieval) without slowing it.
why: Usable supply: depreciated-fab memory becomes productive capacity, leaving fast DRAM for latency-critical jobs.

title: Kerfless exfoliated wafers bypass the Spruce Pine crucible chokepoint
idea: Box[Substrate=epitaxial-lift-off wafer x Fab=porous-Si release on reusable parent x Owner=US wafer startup x Finance=DOE loan]: grow 300 mm epi silicon on a porous release layer, exfoliate it as a DRAM-grade substrate and reuse the CZ parent wafer 10-20 times, cutting crucible-grown ingot demand per DRAM wafer by ~90%.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: removes most high-purity-quartz crucible dependence (>80% Spruce Pine) and lowers wafer cost; enables U.S. substrate supply.

title: Soma floating-body cells on domestic FD-SOI lines
idea: A neuron's soma integrates charge in its body. Capacitorless floating-body cells store holes in the thin SOI body and hold them with FD-SOI back-gate bias, made in existing U.S. 22 nm FD-SOI capacity.
why: 1T cell at ~4-6F2 with no capacitor module, on domestic lines (U.S. manufacturability, capital).

title: Ham radio operator: 32-die stacks talk through inductive coils
idea: A ham operator talks without wires. Stack 32 thinned DRAM dies that pass data through on-die inductive coils (near-field links, ~1 pJ/bit) instead of TSVs, bonded with thin adhesive and powered by edge-plated rails. Any OSAT can assemble them on NAND-style die-stacking lines.
why: Meets the 10x constraint per package footprint: 32 dies is ~10x the bits of 2-4-high packages. Removing TSVs (HBM's ~3x area-per-bit tax and 20-30% yield loss) holds $/GB at commodity DDR level, so this is same cost per bit, not per package.

title: Government-reinsured price-floor insurance for DRAM fab capex
idea: Po: memory prices cannot fall. Fabs buy a policy that pays out when a DRAM price index drops below a cash-cost floor, reinsured by a federal backstop like crop insurance, on condition that the fab keeps its committed capex schedule during the downturn.
why: Trough capex cuts are why shortages arrive 2-3 years later; insured fabs keep building, and lower revenue volatility reduces cost of capital; attacks capital intensity and supply timing.

title: Minify the quality bar: sell grade-B dies with defect maps
idea: Ship dies and HBM stacks that fail full spec with an on-module defect map (bad rows, columns, banks) that the controller or OS maps out badram-style, into AI KV caches, analytics and test tiers.
why: Monetizes the 10-30% yield loss, raising sellable bits per wafer ~10-20% at zero fab cost.

title: CAFE-style tradable memory-efficiency credits for software fleets
idea: Like fuel-economy standards with tradable credits, large cloud and SaaS operators report GB-hours of DRAM per unit of delivered work; those beating a declining fleet target earn credits that laggards must buy.
why: Creates a price signal to write memory-lean software; a 10-20% fleet demand reduction during scarcity is equivalent to adding a large fab.

title: Design-for-harvest clauses in supercomputer and hyperscale procurement
idea: Exascale machines, extreme users, retire after ~5 years holding petabytes of soldered or proprietary memory. DOE, DoD and GSA procurement rules would require standard socketed memory (CAMM2, CXL E3.S) plus a vendor take-back and redeployment plan, so retired memory flows into university and agency clusters.
why: Turns forced obsolescence into a planned secondary supply stream; national labs alone retire multiple PB per cycle.

title: Garage-fab academy: hands-on 2-inch line trains DRAM technicians
idea: Hobbyist garage fabs proved one person can make ICs. A 10-person nonprofit runs a 2-inch, 10 um DRAM teaching line where trainees build working 1T1C arrays end to end, graduating ~200 process technicians a year for new U.S. fabs.
why: Workforce is a time-and-capital chokepoint for U.S. DRAM; this is a cheap pipeline.

title: Aircraft-MRO industry for used DRAM tools plus mothball fab reactivation
idea: Like airline MRO shops that keep 30-year-old jets flying and the Navy's mothball fleet, a U.S. remanufacturing industry overhauls used DUV scanners, etchers and furnaces to as-new spec, paired with a national registry of idle fab shells that can be reactivated for mature DRAM in 18 months.
why: Cuts tool capex 50-70% for mature-node DRAM and reuses existing shells, adding U.S. capacity fast.

title: Rajchman Apertured Ferrite Plates Printed on MLCC Production Lines
idea: Revive Jan Rajchman's 1950s RCA batch-fabricated apertured ferrite plate memory by screen-printing and co-firing nano-ferrite layers with embedded silver drive and sense windings on multilayer-ceramic-capacitor lines (which already print trillions of layered parts a year), giving non-volatile, refresh-free, byte-addressable blocks with ~100-300 ns access.
why: Capital and scarce resources: zero EUV, iron-oxide and silver chemistry, existing MLCC tool base (including U.S. plants); low density but near-zero capex for refresh-free industrial and edge memory that frees DRAM.

title: Magnetostrictive Delay Line Reborn as YIG Magnon Loops on Bubble-Memory Lines
idea: Revive the nickel-wire magnetostrictive delay lines of 1960s calculators as spin-wave (magnon) recirculating loops in yttrium-iron-garnet films grown by the liquid-phase-epitaxy garnet process of 1980s bubble memory: data rides as spin waves with no charge current and is regenerated by a parametric pump each lap.
why: Energy per access: spin-wave propagation costs aJ per bit versus pJ for charge-based bitlines, >=10x net; garnet LPE needs no EUV and little capital.

title: Minify tool cost 30x: open-source fab equipment kits
idea: Fund open-hardware designs for the ALD, sputter, plasma-etch, anneal and nanoimprint tools needed for oxide-semiconductor memory, built from commodity vacuum parts and FPGA controllers at ~1/30 of OEM price, serviced locally, with a shared recipe library.
why: Tools are ~75% of fab capex; ~30x cheaper tools plus ~3x cheaper buildings with litho-free arrays push capital per GB down ~100x and grow a U.S. tool base.

title: No silicon wafer: panel-scale nanoimprint to sub-100 nm rules
idea: Forced limit: glass panels must reach DRAM-like density without EUV. Step-and-repeat nanoimprint templates are pattern-stitched across Gen 6 glass to print sub-100 nm gain-cell features, with die-by-die alignment correcting glass distortion.
why: Density and capital: at 100 nm a Gen 6 panel holds about 1-2 TB, similar to one or two DRAM wafers, with no scanner.

title: Substitute in-house HBM TSV lines with OSAT low-temperature Cu hybrid bonding
idea: Swap memory makers' captive TSV/micro-bump stacking for nanotwinned-Cu hybrid bonding at <=250 C licensed to U.S. OSATs, so packaging houses stack standard DRAM dies into HBM-class stacks.
why: Attacks the HBM TSV tax and 20-30% stack yield loss, and frees memory makers' wafers by moving the stacking step elsewhere.

title: Vinyl-record stamper replication for nanoimprint DRAM array layers
idea: Adapted from record pressing, where electroformed father-mother-son stampers multiply one lacquer master: write one master with U.S. e-beam, electroform many daughter imprint templates, and pattern DRAM's periodic array layers (active, bitline, storage node) by UV nanoimprint in U.S.-built tools.
why: Imprint tools cost ~1/10 of EUV and draw little power; replication amortizes the expensive master, and array redundancy absorbs imprint defects, so array patterning becomes EUV-free and all-U.S. (capital, energy).

title: Minify the die to 2 mm² memory confetti
idea: Cut DRAM into tiny 2 mm² dielets with almost no on-die redundancy, test them in bulk, and place known-good dielets onto carriers by fluidic self-assembly (shape-matched wells in a liquid flow) to build multi-dielet packages.
why: Poisson yield at 2 mm² approaches ~99%, removing most of the 5-10% redundancy area and scrapped large dies; young fabs can ship good bits early in the learning curve.

title: Solder-free, indium-free HBM: copper hybrid bonds plus graphite heat spreaders
idea: A bond needs only atomic contact and Cu interdiffusion, so solder is a crutch: listed elements creep into HBM via indium TIM foils, SnAg bumps and Ta/Co barriers. Stack dies by Cu-Cu/SiCN hybrid bonding with TiN barriers and replace indium TIM with pyrolytic graphite sheets (~1500 W/m-K in plane).
why: HBM TSV tax and scarce resources: bumpless stacking cuts stack height and thermal resistance, raises yield by eliminating bump bridging, and removes In and Ta.

title: Squatter claims airspace: memory tiers in the BEOL above logic dies
idea: An urban squatter occupies unused airspace. Foundries sell a 'memory roof' option: 20 tiers of low-temperature (<400 C) ALD In2O3 2T0C gain cells built in the BEOL above accelerator and CPU logic, so die area already paid for by logic also carries DRAM-class memory and foundries become DRAM suppliers.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: at ~20F^2 per cell with F=20 nm, each tier holds ~15 MB/mm^2, so 20 tiers give ~300 MB/mm^2, ~10x a DDR5 die. The only cost is BEOL deposition, roughly one DRAM wafer's worth per logic wafer, and no separate die, package or PHY is needed.

title: Strategic DRAM Reserve: oil-SPR mechanics applied to memory bits
idea: Fuse the Strategic Petroleum Reserve model with memory. A federal or consortium agency buys standardized DDR5/LPDDR5 dies or wafers in gluts, stores them in nitrogen-dry vaults with periodic rotation, and auctions them in shortages, smoothing the boom-bust that freezes capex.
why: Damping the 4× price swings gives fabs a predictable floor, which lets them commit capacity earlier. It also supplies critical sectors during shocks.

title: Nanoimprint array patterning sidesteps EUV's ruthenium and molybdenum optics
idea: EUV mirrors rely on Mo/Si multilayers with Ru caps, so a Ru-free DRAM cannot lean on EUV. Pattern the periodic array layers by jet-and-flash nanoimprint from fused-silica (Si, O) replica templates cloned from one master, where pattern transfer costs mechanical contact rather than 92 eV photons.
why: EUV single-supplier and capital: NIL tools cost ~1/10 of EUV at ~1/10 the power, and array redundancy absorbs imprint defects.

title: Seed tape: fluidic self-assembly of known-good die onto moving web
idea: Random stimulus 'garden seed tape' -> seeds pre-spaced on paper. Tested DRAM die suspended in liquid fall into shape-matched recesses embossed in a moving polymer web (Alien-RFID-style fluidic assembly), then R2R printing adds RDL and solder to form fan-out packages.
why: Packaging throughput ~10x a pick-and-place or wafer-level fan-out line at a fraction of capex; back-end stops gating memory output.

title: V(D)J recombination: mix-and-match array and periphery chiplets
idea: Immune cells generate diversity by recombining gene segments. Capacitorless array chiplets from many fabs (gain-cell, floating-body, crosspoint) are hybrid-bonded to periphery and controller chiplets from logic fabs through one standard interface, so any fab that can make one segment adds to supply.
why: Unbundling moves the ~49% periphery to cheaper logic nodes and widens the supplier base.

title: GaAs memory's cost death revisited: junction-storage DRAM in RF fabs
idea: GaAs memories (Gigabit Logic, Vitesse SRAMs) died on cost against silicon in the late 1980s-90s. But GaAs's intrinsic carrier density is ~10^4x lower than silicon's, so thermal leakage falls by orders of magnitude: a JFET- or HEMT-access junction-storage DRAM cell built on 6-inch RF GaAs lines (0.25-0.5 um, 1990s-class, largely U.S.-based) could hold charge for very long times with almost no refresh.
why: Refresh and U.S. manufacturability: taps a compound-semiconductor fab pool outside DRAM's chokepoints for low-density, near-refresh-free working memory; density and wafer cost are the main risks.

title: Vertical-channel 4F2 cells at relaxed DUV pitch
idea: Po: density comes from area, not pitch. A vertical-channel transistor with buried bitline and surrounding-gate wordline gives a 4F2 cell; at F=18 nm (reachable by SAQP on ArF immersion) the cell is 1,296 nm2, equal to a 6F2 cell at ~14.7 nm, a node that otherwise needs EUV.
why: Matches next-node density using DUV only; attacks litho capital and EUV dependence.

title: One copy of each AI model per rack via content-addressed pooling
idea: Po: there is only one copy of every model. Inference hosts serving the same open-weight model map its weights read-only from a content-addressed (hash per 2 MB page) CXL memory pool shared across tenants and GPUs, instead of each VM loading its own copy into host DRAM.
why: Popular models are replicated dozens of times per rack in host memory; dedup frees ~30-60% of host DRAM on inference fleets; attacks usable capacity per installed bit.

title: Knudsen-regime hydrogen backside gas replaces helium in etch chucks
idea: Wafer-to-chuck heat transfer at 5-20 Torr is gas-kinetic conduction set by molecular speed and accommodation coefficient, where H2 matches or beats He. Feed chucks with on-site electrolytic H2 at sub-flammable volumes, and texture chuck surfaces to raise H2 accommodation.
why: Backside cooling is one of the largest fab helium uses; switching cuts He demand for etch and implant tools while Qatar's ~30% is offline.

title: Federal Helium Reserve Reborn, With Fab Priority and Recapture Mandates
idea: Re-create the Bush Dome Federal Helium Reserve sold off in 2024 as a strategic semiconductor helium bank: buy North American helium in normal years, re-inject it at Cliffside, release it to fabs under priority rules in shocks, and pair it with grants for closed-loop helium recapture on litho, wafer-cooling and leak-check tools.
why: Scarce resources: Qatar (~30% of supply) offline since March 2026; recapture cuts fab helium use 50-90% and the reserve buffers multi-year disruptions.

title: Sun Proximity Communication Revival: Capacitive Face-to-Face Memory Links
idea: Revive Sun Microsystems' 2004 Proximity Communication, where overlapping chip edges exchanged data through capacitive pads microns apart: DRAM dies overlap the accelerator die edge face-to-face in a shingle, passing signals through ~20 um pads with no bumps, TSVs or large drivers.
why: Energy per bit ~0.1-0.3 pJ versus 3-4 pJ (HBM) and 10-20 pJ (DDR5), >=10x lower; removes the TSV tax (fact 6) so standard DRAM wafers suffice.

title: Mn: Iridium-free Mn3Sn antiferromagnetic memory built on MRAM lines
idea: Store bits in the chiral spin order of Mn3Sn, switched by spin-orbit torque and read through its large anomalous Hall or tunnel signal; no stray fields lets cells pack at sub-20 nm pitch.
why: Abundant Mn and Sn, picosecond switching potential, no Ir/Pt/Co, denser than MRAM.

title: Sequential layer-transfer tiers re-patterned with the same DUV masks
idea: Po: the wafer grows a new wafer every week. After a DRAM array tier is finished, a thin single-crystal Si sheet is transferred on top by ion-cut at <400 C and the same DUV mask set builds the next tier with laser-annealed low-temperature transistors; four tiers quadruple bits per area with no pitch shrink.
why: Density by tier count rather than lithography, reusing one mask set; attacks EUV dependence and cost per bit if per-tier yield exceeds ~95%.

title: Magnetostrictive underfill shakes memory packages free from retired boards
idea: Underfill and solder mask under DRAM packages carry Fe-Co or Ni-ferrite magnetostrictive microparticles; a kHz alternating field makes them strain and heat locally, cracking the interface and softening solder. Packages lift off intact for re-balling without cooking the rest of the board.
why: Today >90% of retired soldered DRAM is shredded; intact harvest adds second-life supply in seconds per board.

title: Open-source DRAM macro compiler for mature logic foundries
idea: Inverts 'DRAM know-how lives inside three companies': publish an open bitcell, sense-amp, refresh-controller and deep-trench/MIM capacitor kit plus compiler for 22-28 nm logic processes so any logic foundry can sell DRAM-class capacity as a standard product.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: taps idle mature-logic capacity with no new tools; density is 5-10x below commodity DRAM, but it diverts embedded and edge demand that today consumes commodity parts.

title: Magnify the prize: $0.10/GB advance market commitment
idea: Governments and AI buyers pledge an advance market commitment to buy the first 10 exabytes of DRAM-class memory (<=100 ns, unlimited endurance via any architecture) at $0.10/GB, plus milestone prizes, modeled on the pneumococcal vaccine AMC.
why: Aims the whole startup and academic ecosystem at exactly 100x cheaper; guaranteed demand de-risks capex for radical processes (panels, R2R, NAND conversion).

title: Wasp nest: 3D-printed concrete fab shells with integrated ducts
idea: Random stimulus 'wasp nest' -> builders that print their own structure. Gantry printers lay the fab shell and the stiff waffle-slab subfab in concrete with printed air-return and utility channels, so ducting is not installed later.
why: Cuts fab construction from ~24 to ~10-12 months and building cost ~20-30%; time and capital are the stated real limits.

title: Linux-LTS frozen DRAM process sold by subscription
idea: Like long-term-support kernel releases, a fab commits a 125 C-qualified DRAM process to a copy-exact freeze for 15 years, with industrial customers paying annual subscriptions that fund spare tools and parts, so products never need requalification.
why: Ends the forced EOL churn that wastes capacity on requalification and hoarding, and monetizes depreciated tools.
